item.title: Would you give AI your credit card?
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: With the release of new AI shopping tools, including from Meta and TikTok, companies are trying to make buying things online even more convenient. Maybe too convenient.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: A growing number of AI agents and tools are now helping you shop until you drop—from recommending products to completing purchases in one click. It’s a bet AI companies and brands hope will pay off big time—but it could also worsen your impulse buying habit.

What happened: Yesterday, TikTok launched an AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout, making it even easier to snap up that viral magnesium supplement on your For You page. These features arrive weeks after Meta’s splashy release of Muse—with one of its key selling points being its ability to shop for you. Other AI companies are rolling out shopping aids, too, like ChatGPT’s new virtual “try on” tool for clothing and accessories.

What makes TikTok’s and Meta’s shopping push especially significant though, is that they already drive a lot of online shopping. Meta is an advertising juggernaut (take Instagram’s eerily specific ads, for example) and runs Marketplace, while 54 million Americans now say they’ve bought something after seeing it in a TikTok video.

Easy to shop…and spend: Agentic shopping’s big draw is that AI can cut the time it takes to find the perfect slow cooker or pair of jeans. But all that convenience also has a potential cost: Swiping your credit card becomes a little too effortless.

Some early adopters say they’re already shopping way more than they did without a robot assistant. And Instinct, another popular AI agent, apparently keeps sending users product recs they didn’t ask for—in one case, it reportedly bought an unneeded bikini without the user’s approval.

Following the money: The agentic shopping spree comes as AI firms face two realities: Running an AI lab is expensive, but few consumers are paying for the tech—only 2.2% of US households had paid AI subscriptions as of May. (OpenAI, for one, is now trying out other ways to boost revenue, like serving ads alongside images its models generate.)

That might be why Meta is leaning so hard into shopping with Muse—since the company expects most users to stick with the free version. It’s angling to eventually profit by taking a small fee on each Muse transaction, but that only works if people get comfortable handing an AI agent their credit card—and let it talk them into buying the $80 sweater they don’t really need.

Bottom line: If AI shopping takes off, it could become a vivid example of why friction is sometimes good—especially when it comes to spending money. —WK

item.title: A brain implant you could get with a shot in your arm
item.dc:creator: Saira Mueller
item.description: An MIT lab is working to make brain implants as simple as a vaccine—and it could eventually lead to human augmentation.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: What if getting a brain implant were as easy as rolling up your sleeve? That’s the pitch Deblina Sarkar, an associate professor at MIT and head of its Nano-Cybernetic Biotrek Lab, made at the conference. Her team is developing microscopic chips that could be injected into the bloodstream before making their own way to the brain. For now, the team is targeting brain cancer (and a few other conditions). But the long game? Upgrading healthy humans.

The pitch: Today’s brain implants require drilling a hole in the skull, which comes with risks like infection, plus roughly $100,000 in surgery costs. This means they can reach fewer than 1% of patients, says Sarkar—and exclude particularly vulnerable ones such as children and the elderly. The implanted electrodes can also kill surrounding neurons. Instead, the lab’s chips skip the operating room entirely and are made of biocompatible materials so the neurons stay healthy, per Sarkar—and treatment could cost under $5,000 at scale.

How it works: These chips, which Sarkar says are a billion times smaller than a grain of rice, hitch a ride on cells before implanting themselves in the target area, where they deliver electrical stimulation that is controlled wirelessly. They can also be switched on and off, says Sarkar, or even built to dissolve after days or years.

The short term: The lab has tested the electrical stimulation part of the tech on mice injected with tumors from the tissue of Mayo Clinic patients—and it extended median survival by more than 50%. Beyond brain cancer, the researchers are also targeting Alzheimer’s, chronic pain, and blindness. To get the tech out of the lab, Sarkar founded Cahira Technologies, and expects to start human trials within three years.

A bionic future: Down the line, Sarkar says the chips could be used in healthy people, too—including for health monitoring. Circulating through the body, they could flag anomalies in individual cells (something an MRI can’t see) before they become full-blown diseases.

In theory, the chips could even optimize how your neurons fire and sync, which Sarkar says would have your brain running at its best. And, like popping an SD card into your device for extra storage, you could even add synthetic neurons. “We do not have to be limited by the 100 billion neurons that biology has provided us,” Sarkar tells us. She’s also not ruling out Matrix-style downloads (kung fu, anyone?), but said the tech and our understanding of the brain have a ways to go before that becomes reality.

Bottom line: If this pans out, the most advanced brain tech on the planet could come with the same aftercare as a flu shot: a Band-Aid and maybe even a lollipop. —SM

item.title: Google’s AI is inescapable in US schools
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: Some schools are trying to restrict AI use—but the pervasiveness of Google’s software and products, including its AI-powered search, is making that difficult.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: A new Wall Street Journal report, based on interviews with more than 60 teachers, school officials, clinicians, parents, and kids, shows how large Google looms in American schools—and how easy it is for students to access the tech giant’s AI tools.

What happened: Some school districts are trying to kick AI out of the classroom, including in New York City and Los Angeles, home to the two largest public school systems in the US.

But there’s a problem with most of these bans: Kids can still use Google Search, where an AI summary and AI Mode chatbot now live at the top of many results’ pages—with Google currently not allowing schools to turn them off. (LA, for its part, says it had to build its own tool to block the Search chatbot.)

As concerns rise over AI use in schools, some parents and educators are looking right at Google, whose products have been fixtures in US classrooms for well over a decade. By the company’s own count, Google’s education software serves over 170 million teachers and students all over the world, and in an informal New York Times poll of teachers last year, 80% said their district handed out Chromebooks to students.

That’s made Google’s products “a critical launchpad for its AI tools to reach kids,” as the WSJ put it—and the world’s most popular search engine might be the jumping off point. AI search summaries are kids’ most widely experienced form of AI, per a March survey from a children’s safety nonprofit, and in a separate test of Google Search, the group found that the integrated AI features completed every homework assignment they typed in. (Google disputes this test’s methodology.)

Google’s long push into education: The company’s influence on US schools stretches well beyond Chromebooks. It also funds teacher AI training and runs a yearlong fellowship that trains superintendents and other school officials on its tech—Gemini included. (Per Google, fellows get no product discounts and aren’t required to use the company’s tools.)

The AI report card so far: As AI spreads through classrooms, some parents, teachers, and students are worried about falling grades and test scores. But the potential risks go beyond AI doing students’ work for them. One Maryland mother learned her teenage daughter had started confiding in Google’s AI, sometimes through the Chromebook her school issued. Gemini apparently told the teen that her mother’s rules around screen time and AI use were “coercive control, emotional abuse, and isolation” and even encouraged her to plot an escape.

Bottom line: Google’s deep reach in schools means that one tech company could have outsized sway over how an entire generation leans on AI to learn—and we’re already seeing the effects. As one teen student said of her AI use: “The Google one was the biggest temptation, because it’s the easiest to access.” —WK

item.title: Is Amazon watching you?
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Choo
item.description: The two biggest delivery networks in the US are bringing cameras along, and you can’t opt out.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: Amazon is rolling out smart glasses with cameras for its delivery drivers, which could be snapping photos every few seconds, and the United States Postal Service (USPS) says it’s starting to test dashcams on mail trucks. In other words, the two delivery services that show up at nearly every home in the US are adding cameras, just as surveillance tech faces growing backlash.

What happened: Amazon’s glasses, unveiled last fall, are meant to help reduce delivery errors by guiding drivers hands-free from van to doorstep—and more than 275,000 deliveries have already been made with them. The company wants 5,000 drivers wearing them by the end of this year and more than 20,000 by the end of 2027, and it’s hoping its eyewear reads less as “pervert glasses” and more as a helpful delivery gadget.

USPS is also getting in on the camera action: it’s testing dashcams on 100 mail trucks around the Washington DC area to spot road conditions and support “community safety.” The pilot was slated to start Sept. 21 and will run for several months.

Smile, you’re on delivery cam: Amazon says the glasses’ photos will feed an AI system to map neighborhoods, and it’ll blur people and vehicle license plates before humans review the images. What it won’t blur is the private property a driver passes on the way to your door. The dashcams on USPS trucks, made by dashcam company Nextbase, start recording as soon as a truck shifts into drive and run for a whole route, scanning everything from roads to sidewalks (they can capture license plates, though they apparently don’t run software to read them).

Destination unknown: Amazon will only use the collected data to “enhance the delivery process,” the exec leading the rollout told Bloomberg. But the company won’t say how long it keeps images, and a spokesperson later confirmed police can get them with a warrant. There’s no way to opt out, either (something the company hasn’t thought about, per the exec). And you won’t be able to see the photos it takes of your place, let alone ask for them to be deleted. USPS is just as vague—it hasn’t said who gets its footage (just USPS, or other government agencies, too?), or how long it’s stored.

Bottom line: Soon, something may be recording you every time a package shows up. But USPS hasn’t shown how its cameras make neighborhoods safer, and Amazon has yet to show how its glasses make deliveries better. Basically, the sentence of the week is “trust me, bro.” —LC

item.title: Apple’s smart home launch is unfashionably late
item.dc:creator: Whizy Kim
item.description: The device, reportedly set to be unveiled on October 13, arrives years after rivals have released similar products—and as Apple’s new CEO eyes a push to ship products faster.
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR: After years of delays, Apple’s long-rumored smart home hub is almost move-in ready. The device is an example of the company’s sometimes sluggish entry into new product categories—something newly minted CEO John Ternus is reportedly trying to fix with a leaner, flatter org.

What happened: The smart home hub, codenamed the very catchy “J490,” will be a roughly 6-inch display that can live on your countertop or be mounted on your wall, according to a new Bloomberg report.

The stationary screen can control all your other smart home gear (like thermostats and door locks) and can also make calls and play music, among other things. A major feature is that it recognizes each person in the house by face or voice and pulls up their own calendar, messages, and apps. Basically, it’s Brady Bunch-approved (though Bloomberg says the face recognition is less reliable than the iPhone’s Face ID). There’s also a guest mode that hides your personal info when neighbors come over.

The hub was supposed to arrive in 2024 alongside a revamped Siri, but its launch was pushed back as the voice assistant’s 2.0 update also faced repeated delays. With a better Siri rolling out this month, J490 is expected to be announced on October 13.

The bigger picture: This much-awaited launch is just one example of an issue that Ternus apparently wants to fix: Apple not moving fast enough. (Besides internal delays, Google and Amazon pretty much have the smart home market locked.) And the pressure to speed up is mounting as Apple faces the perception that it’s lagging in AI, while also dealing with higher component costs and slowing revenue growth in services, which includes subscriptions like iCloud+ and Music.

The Terning point: In order to release new products more often, Apple’s new head honcho wants a leaner company that’s more focused on engineering. He also wants it to get more experimental again.

Step one of that redesign, apparently: fewer managers. Ternus is reportedly weighing whether to shrink some middle-management layers, per Bloomberg, and the company has already cut roles in hardware engineering in recent weeks. These dismissals follow a string of layoffs in other departments, including Siri and Vision Pro, and more could come later this year.

Bottom line: If the smart home hub is a smash hit, Ternus gets credit for something Apple cooked up before he got the top job. If it flops, he has an even stronger case for being leaner and moving faster. —WK

item.title: Protests outside NYC offices of Palantir, Google denounce data centers, facial recognition tech
item.dc:creator: Tricia Crimmins
item.description: The events were part of weeklong anti-Big Tech demonstrations across the US.
item.content:encoded:
Palantir’s unmarked NYC office usually flies under the radar, but it was hard to miss on Wednesday morning when hordes of protesters gathered outside it to condemn the tech company’s work with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The demonstration was a part of a weeklong anti-Big Tech movement percolating across the US, organized by activist groups like Make the Road, United Ratepayers, Food & Water Watch, and People’s Action Institute. “Dump Big Tech” is aimed at tech giants like Palantir, OpenAI, and Google; elected officials in New York, New Jersey, California, Nevada, and Pennsylvania; and data center construction sites in Oregon and West Virginia. The protests point to souring public sentiment surrounding Big Tech, especially ahead of midterm elections.

While each protest is centered on different issues, the event outside Palantir’s offices was squarely focused on the company’s connection with ICE. Speakers at the rally said they’re scared that ICE is using Palantir’s technology to surveil immigrant communities.

“My community has felt a sense of fear that no one should have to feel,” Faith, a youth organizer for Make The Road, an immigrant justice group, told the crowd. (Organizers asked that Faith be identified only by her first name for her safety.) “Palantir working with ICE makes me worry deeply about privacy and about people getting caught up in systems that don’t feel fair, transparent, or humane.”

Because of fears about Palantir using its facial recognition technology against protesters, a majority wore disposable masks, while others wore paper masks decorated with the faces of cartoon characters and superheroes that obscured their entire visage.

“That’s a big fear, that a lot of our data and our identities [will] be tracked by Palantir because we’re here, or because we’re against the violence that ICE is enacting,” Jennifer, a Make the Road organizer who declined to share her surname, told us. “We know that it’s happening across the board, not only to undocumented people. US citizens that are speaking up are being tracked.”

She said she and other protesters hoped the demonstrations encourage elected officials to “look into the contracts” the government has with Big Tech companies and “undo all of the massive surveillance and use of AI that’s only hurting communities.”

NY Assemblymember Claire Valdez, who recently won the Democratic nomination for a US House seat in New York’s 7th Congressional District, also spoke at the rally and offered alternative uses for AI and the advanced technology coming out of companies like Palantir.

“This technology should be used to make our lives better. It should be used to shorten our working hours. It should be used to make our productivity actually pay us more. It should be used to tackle the real emergencies that we are facing right now, like climate change. Instead it is being used by billionaires and tech oligarchs to tear our communities apart,” Valdez said. “We are not going to take it anymore…While Palantir is surveilling us, we are watching them.”

At another demonstration a few blocks away in front of Google’s NYC offices earlier that day, protesters chastised the company for its data centers’ considerable water, energy, and potential fossil fuel usage. Protester Zack Winestine, part of the Rise and Resist direct action group, said he was also demonstrating against “unregulated AI” and Google specifically “forcing people to use AI” when using its search engine.

“AI is not inevitable. There’s all this hype that it can’t be stopped. That’s nonsense. People have agency. People have the right to determine how their lives will be lived and under what circumstances technology functions in their lives,” Winestine told us. “We can affect how these things develop.”

item.title: Google exec says link lists aren’t going away as search transforms
item.dc:creator: Patrick Kulp
item.description: Google VP of Search Liz Reid discussed how the search experience is changing in the AI era and what it means for the internet as a whole.
item.content:encoded:
In recent months, AI has fundamentally changed what it means to google something—and the transformation isn’t done.

The search engine made a slew of announcements at its developer conference earlier this year that included the first change to the search box in a quarter century. The upshot is a more AI-centric experience with options for news alert-style information agents that automatically scour the web for you.

Though Google has clarified that the familiar list of links isn’t going away, multiple headlines have called it the end of search as we know it. But Reid insisted that Google still cares about the health of the internet as a whole.

“Search is not a useful product if the web is not a thriving product, and so I think we probably care about that more than any other company in the world,” Google VP of Search Liz Reid told us.

We spoke with Reid about what this means for how you browse the web, what it means for websites that depend on Google for survival, and how it will change the ads you see.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Do you think that there’s a time in the future, amid all this AI change, that the familiar list of links could go away entirely? Or that there could be a different format for funneling users to the web?

I don’t see any time in which the links go away. I think what we actually see is that people don’t want AI or the web; they want both. There’s a lot of topics where AI really gets you started, and then people want to engage more. They value the expertise, the opinions, the taste of how to think about a particular topic. This is a time in which AI is growing, and it’s a time in which newsletters and podcasts and videos and all these new formats seem to also be blossoming because people really want to hear that expertise. So we want to continue to make that thrive.

We have for a long time continued to innovate on how you can surface links on the web. So we have the blue links, but we have, at times, we have the top stories part. We have what people are saying in AI Mode and in AI Overviews.

If we know users want to connect to that information, how do we make it as easy as possible? How do we make it as seamless as possible? And we’ll continue to innovate and we announced some updates pretty recently on how we’re showcasing links in additional ways. But I think that is kind of what makes search at its heart—not just knowing the information about the web, but connecting people to content on the web. And I don’t see that going away.

Obviously, online publishers are seeing click-through rates decline with these changes, and some publishers are even considering blocking all Google crawlers. In terms of making sure that the open web is still a healthy place to supply these AI tools and search, how do you think about that in the long term?

We do spend a lot of time thinking about this. We try to really design our AI experiences in sort of a web-forward way. We have teams whose job is to think about: What are great links to surface more effectively? How do you show them in a way that’s great for folks? We’ve innovated; one example is in AI Overviews, we’ll now often show on some timely stories, a big carousel of publishers that we didn’t have three months ago. So we’re constantly trying to figure out how we innovate on that.

The good news is that people still want to connect with other people’s content, and so we can facilitate that. And as long as people make great content that other people want to read, then we believe we can continue to foster that.

Companies like Microsoft are experimenting with publisher marketplaces or other compensation schemes. Is that something you’re considering?

We have a blog post in which we’ve talked about some of the various news deals and other things we have.

We have a variety of different ways—we have a long history of deals with news and others for great content. In general, we’re all still—I mean, at times it can feel like a long time—but we’re still pretty early in the space, and so continue to innovate.

In terms of the revenue side, how has this changed Google’s ad model? Do you feel like you’ve kind of cracked advertising in generative AI?

What we are seeing is as people ask longer queries, they’re specifying more of their intent. What are they really trying to do? What’s important to them? And that sort of allows new opportunities to think about ads targeting.

There’s some efforts like direct offers, in which…the advertiser can give a more specific ad for you based on what it is. And so, an example is like you’re searching for a hotel, you’re searching with a family. Maybe a hotel wants to offer free breakfast. They’re not going to give free breakfast to the person that they think is traveling for business who will just pay, or they won’t eat. But this family might pick that hotel because of it, and so Google’s system will allow [the hotel] to say, “Oh, I have a special discount just for you for breakfast,” and that really provides new value to the user and sort of allows the hotel to get additional visitors. We both have something that’s working, and there’s lots of room for innovation going forward.

There’s always been some level of slop on the internet, and I know Google has tools to sift through that. But as generative AI tools have created this ability to churn out more content, how do you make sure that with things like the AI Overviews, the accuracy is maintained? And have you seen the accuracy of those go up overall?

To your point, there’s always been slop. Sometimes people are like, “Oh, there’s now slop on the web.” In my experience, there’s been slop for 20 years. So we have a lot of experience and teams whose job is to ensure that both we’re getting rid of spam and that that rarely surfaces, and that high-quality content continues to surface. And when we do AI Overviews or AI Mode, we actually make use of those underlying search ranking systems so that it’s the highest-quality sites going into AI Overviews. Overall, the quality of the AI Overviews has continued to improve and has improved considerably since we first launched. The models are much better, for one, so that really helps. But also, we’ve just learned a lot and continue to grow on what the techniques are [and] how you work with the models to ensure that you can actually really ground the data in high-quality information.

Are Gemini and AI Mode search still different experiences, or are they converging into the same thing?

We think of them as having two different North Stars. Gemini is really focused on being this assistant, and search AI Mode is really focused on a generative AI search experience. And so for search, that means the importance of connecting to the web is vital. And so the way that we show the web is different…we tend to focus on information use cases more heavily. Versus with Gemini, we’ll focus on a lot of productivity and creativity use cases.

The use cases overlap. We have a view that you should meet users where you are, so you don’t go and say, like, “Oops, you asked the question in the wrong product. Try again.” We will try and answer across both of them the full breadth of questions that come to our products, but we will tune them differently, and really tune search to focus on optimizing for information use cases and optimizing for connecting people to the web.

Where is Google search headed in the long term, and what are some of the biggest ways we can expect it to change further?

There’s a couple of things that we see. Experiences are becoming more personal and custom for you, for each one. It’s not just that you can ask that longer question, but that we start to understand how to make information most useful for you. We see people learn differently. We have people who love videos and people who hate videos. We have people who are experts in the financial jargon and not in the medical jargon. We have people who speak different languages.

And so, with some of the things like generative UI…the job is not just for you to technically access information, but for it to be useful to you—that’s an important part of the mission. How do we present information in ways that are much more useful? That sense of building a thing that feels designed for you, and not just designed for 2 billion people, to make it easier for you to understand and grasp the information will continue.

Also, agents and how they show up in search in terms of just, how do they offload more of the work you don’t want to do? I think people have parts of searching where they enjoy and they’re delighted, and then they have parts of tasks that feel like there’s a lot of toil. And so, how can you offload those parts, and then make it easy for people to spend their time on the things they want to enjoy?

We’ll see that people will ask harder and harder questions. That’s been the evolution of search. You get better at answering the question. They’re like, “OK, I’m gonna raise the bar on you,” and so I think we’ll continue to see people go more and more to, what’s the real question they’re trying to get done, what’s the task they’re trying to get done.

item.title: This startup wants a robot to change your tires
item.dc:creator: Jordyn Grzelewski
item.description: One of the problems ATI aims to help solve is a growing shortage of automotive service technicians.
item.content:encoded:
Getting your car’s tires changed is the automotive service equivalent of getting a root canal.

That’s how Andy Chalofsky, CEO of newly launched AI and robotics company Automated Tire, Inc., or ATI, thinks of it—and why he and his fellow co-founders decided to use an emerging technology to disrupt a process that’s historically been cumbersome, time-consuming, and physically demanding.

“While the auto industry has made great strides with advanced technologies over recent decades, automotive service bays have seen little innovation to match,” Chalofsky said in a statement Tuesday announcing ATI’s emergence from stealth.

“Most notably, electric vehicles wear through tires up to 30% faster,” he added. “The proliferation of EVs creates significantly more tire service opportunities, but tire technician jobs are dirty, injury-prone, and difficult to fill.”

Get smart: Enter SmartBay, ATI’s platform that uses robotics, machine learning, and computer vision to automate services including tire changes, wheel balancing, and vehicle inspections. The startup touts SmartBay as a way to increase repair shops’ efficiency, improve the customer experience, and help solve a nagging automotive technician shortage.

Here’s how it works: Once a vehicle is in position, the platform automatically begins an inspection. It analyzes tire and wheel conditions while gathering diagnostic data. “The robotic system then executes the tire change and wheel balancing process, removing and reinstalling tires with consistent accuracy while simultaneously calculating and applying precise wheel weights to ensure optimal balance,” according to a news release.

According to ATI, SmartBay allows one technician to manage up to three service bays at a time, reducing the time for a full tire service job by half. The product fits within a standard 12-foot service bay.

So tire-d: Chalofsky represents the fourth generation of his family to work in the tire business. He started working in tire distribution and went on to establish an online tire retailer that he later sold. In 2020, he said, he started to think about the next industry challenge he wanted to focus on.

“We just saw that there was a real need in installation, and tire changing and wheel balancing,” he told us. “It’s not a very pleasurable customer experience. We would talk to the shops and the shops would oftentimes talk about how hard it was to get labor.”

ATI cited a report from the National Automotive Dealers Association identifying a shortage of 37,000 automotive service technicians. This shortage affects drivers, ATI argued, by leading to “inconsistent service quality and even more grueling wait times.”

“We’re making not only that technician more efficient—we’re making them more profitable for them and the shop. And we’re also making it an easier job with a lower threshold of skill,” Chalofsky said. “You’re now taking the workforce and you’re allowing them to fill in the gap a little bit and do a job they’d actually rather do.”

He noted that repair shops and dealers employ highly skilled mechanics who are trained to work on vehicles that are becoming ever more complex. Rather than having these skilled workers do tire changes and vehicle inspections, they can focus on more lucrative and specialized service jobs.

“By segmenting that work, we’re allowing those…technicians to really focus on the more complicated vehicles and the more complicated problems,” Chalofsky said.

Problem, meet solution: Chalofsky believes that starting with a problem, then devising a solution, differentiates ATI’s approach from other tech startups.

“The most common tech story is these smart people that are into robotics or into engineering. They’re solving problems, and then they’re taking it to an industry to try to get a product-market fit,” he said. “The thing that defines us is the opposite: We have robotics and engineering talent, of course, but are really founded with deep automotive tire expertise. And we focused on solving a problem and bringing engineering to that problem, rather than engineering and then trying to bring the industry to the problem.”

item.title: Is it really the end of SaaS as we know it?
item.dc:creator: Patrick Kulp
item.description: New AI agent and coding tools have triggered a “SaaS-pocalypse” narrative. The reality is more complicated.
item.content:encoded:
Are software companies like Oracle and Salesforce headed for the trash icon of history?

Investors have been dumping their stocks in software-as-a-service (SaaS) companies since late January, with one trader (and dozens of headlines) dubbing it the “SaaS-pocalypse.” So while time will tell whether the end is actually nigh, change is in the air. And like seemingly all things business-related in 2026, that change is predicated on some form of AI.

The prevailing theory behind the sell-offs seems to be that sophisticated workplace agents as well as new coding tools from Anthropic and OpenAI could make this sort of business software model obsolete. If an IT team can easily “vibe code” internal software or assign tasks to role-specific plug-ins within Claude Cowork, do they still need expensive pay-per-seat platform subscriptions?

“The thing with agentic systems is now you can have agents just read your business policies and generate the software,” Booz Allen chief technology officer Bill Vass told us. “This is going to disintermediate these SaaS vendors and these ERP vendors. The market just realized that, and that’s the reason you see the big reaction.”

SaaS leaders claim a lot happens behind the scenes of these platforms that their customers can’t easily replicate, such as data governance and security and teams of developers that ensure that software works reliably. But business leaders at companies like Walmart and LiveRamp have told us they’re now building more internal tools and doing so more quickly than ever, if not yet severing SaaS contracts.

What nobody denies is that the SaaS industry is in a period of flux, and companies need to continually evolve to keep offerings competitive.

This sentiment is not exactly new. For instance, when we spoke a year ago with Scott Snyder, senior fellow at the Wharton School, he warned that SaaS companies could struggle to keep up with AI development tools.

“People could say, ‘Well, why am I using a service—[like] a Salesforce customer service bot—when I can just build my own at a very low cost because I’ve already got the AI infrastructure set up?’” Snyder said last March. “If the switching costs aren’t that high, these larger companies may roll out their own, and I think that’s going to be the interesting tension going forward.”

A major evolution

In a way, what comes next could harken back to an earlier model of business software development, according to Vass. Before standardized enterprise resource planning (ERP) software platforms became widespread in the 1990s—a precursor to SaaS—businesses mostly used custom-built internal software, Vass said.

“Originally, we all built custom ERP systems for everyone. So you did it exactly the way the Army wanted…or exactly the way Bank of America wanted, or exactly the way BMW wanted,” Vass said. “Then there was this move that, ‘Well, gee, that’s really expensive to build all those custom systems. Let’s all standardize on SAP or PeopleSoft or Oracle.’…It was very painful to go through that, and every single business person hated it.”

Vass said that the rise of AI agents and coding tools could swing the pendulum back toward more individual customization.

Still, Vass said he thinks many SaaS vendors will likely successfully pivot to selling AI agents, and internal agentic systems haven’t matured to the point where he’s seen companies actually cutting SaaS contracts.

“You’re going to have a combination of people that are going to just build their own agentic, if you like, ERP systems that will still be running on a cloud, probably, but run [on premises], too,” Vass said. “You’ll have others that will say, ‘I’ll just go use Agentforce from Salesforce,’ for example, or something like that, which is an agentic system to do what I do. And then it’s a lot more flexible.”

Those contracts may soon be changing form, however. Faisal Masud, who heads HP’s digital and lifecycle services division within the company’s SaaS business, said that the traditional seat- and usage-based models for pricing SaaS platforms are “evolving.” Masud said HP is mulling an additional option for outcome-based pricing based on metrics like number of tickets eliminated or hardware procurement costs.

“We’re considering, as the market evolves, to have both seat-based and outcome-based pricing models,” Masud said.

Enterprise SaaS price increases have been significantly outpacing CIO budgets in recent months, according to Gartner research, with companies often facing 10% to 20% hikes during contract renewals. Gartner expects enterprise software spending to increase by 15% this year, but much of it will go toward price increases and AI infrastructure spend, per the B2B-focused hub SaaStr.

The average annual contract value for private SaaS companies has trended upward in recent years, jumping from a median of $22,357 to $26,265 between 2023 and 2024, according to a survey of more than 1,000 respondents conducted by lending firm SaaS Capital.

Masud said the SaaS market is in for a correction rather than a full-on doomsday scenario. He said smaller point solutions for specialized use cases—“you can guess what those are”—are more likely to be impacted than larger, more integrated platforms. He predicted the biggest effect will be drops in pricing as CIOs negotiate better deals.

“Having built a SaaS company, we were users of SaaS, too…And some of those prices were just completely out of bounds for us and for the economic buyers. Everything was very expensive,” he said.

Back-SaaS

In early February, two CNBC reporters with no coding experience vibe-coded a clone of a dashboard from project-management platform Monday.com in under an hour to demonstrate the threat that SaaS companies face. The result was a working prototype that the reporters said could successfully manage their personal lives. If reporters could vibe-code their way through a dashboard, what then of the multibillion-dollar SaaS companies?

Alexey Korotich, chief product officer at workplace platform Wrike, a competitor of Monday.com, said it’s been easy to build dashboards like that for years—the user interface part of the SaaS offering is already heavily commoditized. What’s harder to replicate, he said, are data governance, back-end infrastructure, and reliability.

“Yes, you can build a whiteboard dashboard in an hour or so, but then, how does that look if you start adding features? How does that look if you start finding bugs here and there?” Korotich said. “You will quickly realize that it’s beyond your capacity to handle. It’s not one person’s job, it’s a team’s job to actually take care of this whole thing.”

Tamar Yehoshua, chief product and AI officer at Atlassian, the company behind platforms like Jira, Rovo, and Trello, said the AI transformation will likely be similar to how cloud services changed software tools, but at an accelerated pace. Cloud services first gave rise to SaaS in the aughts as subscription models replaced traditional perpetual licenses.

“SaaS is not going away,” she said. “People are going to have to build software. People are going to have to communicate with other people. Unless you think that every organization is going to be one person who’s just shooting off an AI.”

Not everyone agrees that the “SaaS-pocalypse” is an overreaction, however. Tatyana Mamut, a former Salesforce VP who now runs a startup called Wayfound that partners with Salesforce on agent monitoring, expects the SaaS market to majorly shrink over the next half-decade.

This outcome would contradict various market research reports that show the SaaS industry continuing to grow significantly in the next decade amid an ongoing AI transformation.

AI will eliminate the primary switching costs of retraining humans (since much of the work will be done by agents) and restructuring data (because LLMs don't require structured data), she said. Reductions in seats required for most SaaS subscriptions will also eat into profits, she said.

“The way we’re going to know who’s going to be alive in 2030 is to see who launches really great AI agents that are doing full and complete jobs this year in 2026,” Mamut said. “That’s my best bet.”
